doc.title: Harold Ousley interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: Jack McDuff and songwriting
summary: Ousley describes working with McDuff and Lew Futterman's publishing and how he writes from the horn, with hits like Return of the Prodigal Son.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: And gosh, you made quite a bit of music with Jack McDuff.

Oh yeah. Jack and I met in Chicago because he lived there at the time. And he had a small band that we used to work with and rehearse. So that was my first time playing with Jack. And then when I came to New York and Jack came through I was affiliated with a gentleman named Lew Futterman that had a publishing company. So he would record a lot of the songs in the publishing company. And so McDuff recorded about three or four songs of mine, and then I recorded some other music. I had quite a few other songs that got recorded at that time.
Yeah, you’ve done quite a bit of writing. Do you sit at a keyboard when you write? Or how does it evolve? © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -17-

No, I write from a horn. I’ll hear a song and when I hear it, if I feel good or get that feeling about it then I go to my horn and play it and then put it on tape so I don’t forget it. And then just kind of develop it from that point. Because a lot of times a song will just keep coming back to me, you know, and so I may write it and it may take me maybe, instead of writing it in one day or one sitting it is from time to time and I get little pieces here and then I get the completeness of the song. And then if it’s a song I think it’d be nice to have a lyric to this. Then I start working on a lyric for it. But that’s just basically how I write.
Has it ever happened where the lyric comes first for you?

No I always write instrumentally first. Yeah because I don’t really consider myself a lyricist. But I’ve tried to do this because I want to get my songs done by vocalists as well so it’s good to have a lyric.
Yeah. Another iron in the fire.

Yeah, yeah. Now on “Return of the Prodigal Son” I had several recordings on. Freddie Hubbard did it, George Benson did it. I was working with Ray Bryant at the time at Minton’s as a matter of fact and he was getting ready to do some recordings so I wrote it for that particular recording. But Stanley Turrentine did it. So I had about seven or eight recordings on it.
